name: FSST (Fast Static Symbol Table)
workload: Compression of short strings (22 'dbtext' data sets, each an 8 MB file, single-threaded) with random access per string; LZ4 used in file-based mode.
claimed_speedup: PVLDB 2020 paper Table 1: compression speed FSST higher than LZ4 on most sets (e.g. genome 1,307 vs 566 MB/s, uuid 1,113 vs 632, credentials 984 vs 439) with higher compression factor (e.g. genome 3.32 vs 1.59, uuid 2.44 vs 1.55); decompression speed similar to LZ4 on average (e.g. genome 2,838 vs 1,126 MB/s, hex 1,546 vs 1,891, urls 2,296 vs 2,264). tradeoffs: Strings only (symbol table of up to 8-byte symbols mapped to 1-byte codes); static table per block, random access to single strings without block decode; not a general-purpose byte-stream compressor. Best on short-string columns, ratio gain largest on machine-generated IDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (PVLDB vol 13 no 12, 2020); numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (via raw.githubusercontent.com). LZ4 version is old (1.8.1) and gcc 8.3.1. Decompression is roughly on par with LZ4, not faster; the main win is ratio plus random access, and compression speed. name: FastPFor (FastPFOR C++ library)
baseline: Simple-8b and VByte (as measured in the TurboPFor README table)
workload: Same TurboPFor icapp ZIPF benchmark (100M Zipfian integers): FP_SimdFastPFor 64Ki block decode vs Simple-8b and FP_VByte
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'can decode at least 4 billions of compressed integers per second ... 15 GB/s', 'significantly faster than generic codecs like gzip, LZO, Snappy or LZ4'. Third-party table (TurboPFor README, ZIPF): FP_SimdFastPFor 8748 MB/s decode vs Simple-8b 3832 (~2.3x, derived from page data) and vs FP_VByte 4268 (~2.0x, derived from page data); encode 624 MB/s is slower than Simple-8b 848.
stars_or_usage: 978 stars; DuckDB derived code from it; Lucene 4.6 PForDelta format derived from FastPFOR
tradeoffs: Research library for 32-bit integers (64-bit coverage is partial); SSSE3 minimum for key codecs, NEON on aarch64; no input validation during decode (documented); best codecs need 128-integer or larger blocks (FastPFor itself needs larger blocks than SIMD binary packing).
caveats: The repo README claims are against gzip/LZO/Snappy/LZ4 (not in the baseline list). The Simple-8b and VByte comparison is derived from a competitor's table that gives no flags; encode speed of SimdFastPFor is lower than Simple-8b in that table. The SPE 2015 paper 'Decoding billions of integers per second through vectorization' (peer reviewed, seen only as a WebSearch snippet because arXiv and Wiley were blocked) is the primary evidence and was not opened. Note FastPFor is itself the baseline other catalog entries beat.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ SIMD integer compression bit packing faster than FastPFor varint github'; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
